items.heading: Dish or curry turned out too salty
details: Add a peeled raw potato or two, simmer for 10-15 minutes, then remove it - it absorbs excess salt.
Stir in a spoon of curd, cream, or coconut milk to dilute and balance the flavor.
Add a pinch of sugar or a squeeze of lemon to help mask the saltiness.
Dilute a gravy with extra water or stock and simmer briefly to reheat.
For rice or pulao, mix in a portion of freshly cooked, unsalted rice.

items.heading: Dish is too spicy or has too much chili
details: Stir in curd, cream, milk, or coconut milk to mellow the heat.
Add a spoon of sugar, jaggery, or honey to balance the burn.
Add extra chopped vegetables, potato, or paneer to dilute the chili per serving.
Squeeze in lemon, or add a little tamarind, to shift the balance away from heat.
Serve with plain rice, yogurt raita, or bread to offset spice at the table.

items.heading: Dish turned out too sour
details: Add a pinch of sugar or jaggery to round off the sourness.
Stir in a spoon of cream, coconut milk, or ghee to mellow it.
Add a little extra of the base (onion-tomato masala, dal, or stock) to dilute it.
Simmer a few extra minutes uncovered - sourness often mellows with more cooking.

items.heading: Dish turned out too sweet
details: Add a squeeze of lemon or a splash of vinegar to cut through the sweetness.
Stir in a pinch of salt to rebalance the flavor.
Add a little chili or black pepper for contrast.
Dilute with more of the unsweetened base ingredients.

items.heading: Dish tastes bitter (burnt garlic, bitter gourd, overcooked greens)
details: Add a spoon of sugar or jaggery to counter the bitterness.
Stir in cream, curd, or coconut milk to round out the flavor.
Add lemon juice or tamarind for tang, which distracts from bitterness.
If the spices or garlic are burnt, do not scrape the pan - start the tempering again in a fresh pan if possible.

items.heading: Gravy or milk-based curry has curdled
details: Take it off the heat immediately to stop further curdling.
Blend the gravy briefly with a hand blender to smooth it out.
Whisk in a spoon of besan (gram flour) or cornflour slurry and simmer to bring it back together.
For milk-based curries, add the curdled portion back gradually while whisking on low heat with a splash of fresh milk.

items.heading: Rice turned out sticky or mushy
details: Spread the cooked rice on a wide plate or tray to release excess steam and moisture.
Fluff gently with a fork rather than stirring, which mashes the grains.
Next time, rinse rice well before cooking to remove surface starch, and use the correct water ratio.
Leftover sticky rice works well repurposed as fried rice, which hides the texture.

items.heading: Rice is undercooked or hard
details: Sprinkle a little hot water over the rice, cover tightly, and steam on low heat for 5-10 more minutes.
Avoid opening the lid repeatedly, which lets steam escape.
If using an open pot, add a splash more water next time - the water level was likely too low.

items.heading: Dal or lentils will not soften
details: Add salt only after the dal is soft - salt added too early can slow softening.
A small pinch of baking soda in the water speeds up softening (use sparingly, it affects texture).
Keep cooking with enough hot water topped up as needed; hard water or older lentils take longer.
Switch to a pressure cooker to finish it off quickly if it has been simmering too long on an open pot.

items.heading: Chapati or roti dough too sticky
details: Dust hands and the dough lightly with dry flour and knead again.
Let the dough rest covered for 15-20 minutes - it firms up as the gluten relaxes.
Add flour gradually, a tablespoon at a time, rather than all at once.

items.heading: Chapati or roti dough too dry and cracking
details: Wet your hands with a little water and knead the dough again.
Add water a teaspoon at a time until the dough turns smooth and pliable.
Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 10-15 minutes before rolling.

items.heading: Rotis turning out hard
details: Knead the dough longer and rest it covered for at least 20-30 minutes before rolling.
Roll evenly, not too thin, and cook on a well-heated tawa.
Store cooked rotis wrapped in a cloth or insulated box to keep them soft.

items.heading: Cake did not rise, or turned out dense
details: Check that the baking powder or soda was fresh and measured accurately.
Do not overmix the batter once flour is added - this develops gluten and makes it dense.
Make sure the oven was fully preheated before the cake went in.
Avoid opening the oven door during the first two-thirds of the baking time.

items.heading: Cake stuck to the pan
details: Run a thin knife or spatula gently around the edges to loosen it.
Place a warm, damp cloth under the pan for a minute to loosen the base.
Next time, grease the pan well and line the base with parchment or butter paper.

items.heading: Vegetables turned overcooked and soggy
details: Cook covered for less time, or add vegetables in stages, hardier ones first.
Shock blanched vegetables in cold water immediately to stop the cooking.
Repurpose overcooked vegetables into a soup, mash, or paratha stuffing.

items.heading: Meat turned out tough
details: Simmer it longer on low heat in some liquid or gravy - tough cuts soften with slow cooking.
Pressure cook for a few extra whistles to tenderize it quickly.
Slice against the grain before serving to make it easier to chew.
Next time, marinate with curd, raw papaya paste, or lemon juice beforehand to tenderize.

items.heading: Fried food turned out soggy, not crisp
details: Fry in small batches so the oil temperature does not drop.
Drain fried items on a wire rack instead of paper towels, so steam can escape from below too.
Make sure the oil is hot enough before adding food - it should sizzle immediately.
Pat food dry before frying to remove excess surface moisture.

items.heading: Onions browning too fast or burning
details: Lower the flame and stir more frequently.
Add a pinch of salt early on - it helps onions release moisture and cook evenly.
If already burnt, discard the burnt bits and start again rather than continuing with a bitter base.

items.heading: Garlic burnt while tempering
details: Remove the pan from the heat immediately.
Discard the burnt garlic and oil if heavily blackened, as it turns bitter.
Start the tempering again in fresh oil on a lower flame, adding garlic later in the sequence.

items.heading: Gravy or sauce turned out too thin
details: Simmer uncovered on low-medium heat to reduce and thicken it naturally.
Mix a spoon of cornflour or besan with cold water into a smooth slurry and stir it in while simmering.
Mash a few cooked vegetables or lentils from the dish itself and stir back in to thicken.

items.heading: Gravy or sauce turned out too thick
details: Add hot water, stock, or milk a little at a time while stirring, and simmer briefly.
Re-check and adjust seasoning after diluting, since the flavor gets diluted too.

items.heading: Too much oil floating on curry
details: Skim it off the surface gently with a spoon.
Lay a paper towel briefly on the surface to soak up excess oil, then remove it.
Chill the curry - the solidified fat can then be lifted off the top before reheating.

items.heading: Mayonnaise or a sauce emulsion has broken
details: Start fresh with a new egg yolk (or a teaspoon of mustard and water) in a clean bowl.
Whisk continuously and add the broken mixture back in very gradually to help it re-emulsify.

items.heading: Preventing cut potatoes from browning
details: Submerge peeled or cut potatoes in a bowl of water until ready to cook.
Add a few drops of lemon juice or vinegar to the water for extra protection.

items.heading: Ripening fruit faster (mango, banana, avocado)
details: Place the fruit in a paper bag with a ripe banana or apple - the ethylene gas speeds ripening.
Store at room temperature, not in the fridge, until ripe.
Wrapping the fruit in newspaper and keeping it in a warm spot also helps.

items.heading: Keeping bananas fresh longer
details: Wrap the crown or stem area tightly in cling film to slow the release of ripening gas.
Store bananas separately from other fruits like apples and mangoes.
Refrigerate once ripe - the peel darkens, but the fruit inside stays fine for longer.

items.heading: Preventing cut avocado from browning
details: Brush the exposed surface with lemon or lime juice.
Store with the pit still in and press cling film directly onto the cut surface before refrigerating.

items.heading: Reviving stale bread
details: Sprinkle lightly with water and warm it in an oven or on a tawa for a few minutes.
Toast slices directly for a crisp texture instead.
Repurpose stale bread into croutons, bread crumbs, or a bread pudding.

items.heading: Getting rid of a raw flour smell in gravies
details: Cook the flour or slurry on low-medium heat for a few extra minutes, stirring constantly, until the raw smell disappears.
Dry-roast besan lightly before using it in gravies to remove the rawness upfront.

items.heading: Removing onion or garlic smell from hands
details: Rub hands on a stainless steel object, such as a spoon or the sink, under running water for 30 seconds.
Wash with lemon juice, salt, or a little vinegar, then rinse.
Follow with regular dish soap to remove any residual smell.

items.heading: Removing fish smell from hands or utensils
details: Rub hands with lemon juice, vinegar, or salt before washing with soap.
Wash utensils with a vinegar-water rinse, then regular dish soap.
Boil a slice of lemon or a splash of vinegar in water on the stove to clear fish smell from the kitchen air.
